__map_ecological__.name: Ecological Conservation Priorities
__map_ecological__.description: Every layer below combined into one map of ecological importance. Each area takes the importance of the highest-ranked layer covering it, so overlaps never add up. Hover an area to see which layers apply; click it for the records behind them.

__map_agricultural__.name: Agricultural Conservation Priorities
__map_agricultural__.description: Thetford's important farmland soils, ranked by NRCS crop-production score and whether the land is open today: top-rated soil on open land ranks highest, productive soil elsewhere lowest, the other two in between. The layers never overlap; hover any area to see which applies.

custom_3b424511.name: Amphibian Road Crossings
custom_3b424511.goal: Keep spring migration routes between wintering forest and breeding pools passable, and keep the roadside habitat at those spots intact.
custom_3b424511.motivation: Thetford's 2025 wildlife road crossing study found 24 biologically active amphibian crossings totaling 3.7 miles, with eight species recorded. Two are Species of Greatest Conservation Need: spotted salamander, at eight crossings, and four-toed salamander (ranked S3, uncommon in Vermont) at one. Adults cross on a handful of wet nights each spring, so a single busy stretch of road can erase a local population. See the Thetford Conservation Commission for the full inventory.
custom_3b424511.how_built: The crossings the 2025 Thetford wildlife road crossing study rated high or average for amphibian connectivity (18 of its 24), buffered 300 ft.

custom_f986b655.name: Confirmed Vernal Pools
custom_f986b655.goal: Protect pools with confirmed breeding activity together with the forest immediately around them.
custom_f986b655.motivation: Fishless seasonal pools are the main breeding habitat for wood frogs and for Vermont's mole salamanders — spotted, blue-spotted and Jefferson — which breed nowhere else. The animals spend most of the year in the surrounding forest, not the water, so protecting the pool alone does not work. Vermont Fish & Wildlife manages that forest out to 600 ft (Wildlife Habitat Management: A Landowner’s Guide). The 600 ft outer zone is the buffer mapped here. The 11 pools shown are those the Vermont Vernal Pool Atlas lists as confirmed in Thetford.

custom_c2ea57e7.name: Natural Communities
custom_c2ea57e7.goal: Protect the rare and uncommon natural community types confirmed in town.
custom_c2ea57e7.motivation: Vermont recognizes 97 wetland and upland natural community types and conserving good examples of each is a cornerstone of the state's strategy for biological diversity (Vermont Fish & Wildlife natural community fact sheets). This layer holds the rare (S2) and uncommon (S3) types mapped in Thetford: Wet Clayplain Forest and Sugar Maple Riverine Forest on the glacial clays of the valley floors, an Intermediate Fen, Northern Hardwood Seepage Forest and Alluvial Shrub Swamp. Others are known to occur but have not yet been mapped. Small in acreage, disproportionate in value. Records come from the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory.

custom_0cf3cd91.name: Endangered and Threatened Species
custom_0cf3cd91.goal: Protect documented habitat for species listed as threatened or endangered.
custom_0cf3cd91.motivation: Ten recorded occurrences of species protected under Vermont or federal endangered species law: nine animals and one plant. Four are listed federally as well as by the state, six by the state alone. The state withholds which species each occurrence is, so that rare species cannot be tracked down from a public map (Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory). Thetford's Natural Resource Inventory names the listed species known in town: the northern long-eared bat (federally endangered), little brown and eastern small-footed bats, the federally endangered dwarf wedgemussel in the Connecticut River, and the state-threatened plant sweet coltsfoot. The bats use the town's forests, wetlands and riverbanks from mid-April through October, which is why the state asks landowners to avoid cutting trees in those months (Vermont Fish & Wildlife).
custom_0cf3cd91.how_built: Occurrences in the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory (public version, data current to October 2026) of species listed as threatened or endangered by Vermont, the federal government, or both. Shapes are drawn exactly as the state publishes them, with no added buffer. About half are circles around a single observation, sized to how precisely it was located; the state notes a population may extend beyond what is mapped (Natural Heritage data guidelines).

custom_0a14cdde.name: Top Tier Crossings
custom_0a14cdde.goal: Keep passable the best-rated road crossings on the town's most important road sections.
custom_0a14cdde.motivation: Crossings on road sections the 2025 Thetford wildlife road crossing study classified as regionally important, carrying wildlife movement along corridors that run well beyond town, or locally important, linking forest blocks of 500 acres or more outside the regional networks. Each was also rated above average or better for connectivity. Keeping forest cover on both shoulders of the road is what keeps them passable.
custom_0a14cdde.how_built: Crossings from the study, tiered by its road-section class and its connectivity rating for each crossing. On regionally or locally important sections, above average or better is highest importance, average is medium, and below average is important; on potentially regionally important sections, each rating sits one tier lower. Only crossings within 100 ft of a priority or highest priority forest connectivity block are included, kept whole and buffered 100 ft. Crossings rated well below average, those on unclassified sections, and underpasses are left out.

custom_2bbc6497.name: Other Wetlands
custom_2bbc6497.goal: Treat every other mapped wetland and its 50 ft margin as land where change needs care.
custom_2bbc6497.motivation: Wetlands store floodwater, filter runoff and support a disproportionate share of Vermont's rare species. Thetford's are mostly small, common types, easy to lose one at a time. Every state-mapped wetland in town is Class II, so most work in one or its 50 ft buffer needs a permit under the Vermont Wetland Rules (Vermont DEC). Vermont has lost as much as 35% of its original wetlands (Vermont DEC).
custom_2bbc6497.how_built: The Vermont Significant Wetlands Inventory, mostly remapped in 2024, buffered 50 ft, minus Important Wetlands and its buffer.

custom_77a73964.name: Highest Priority Connectivity Blocks
custom_77a73964.goal: Keep the forest network unfragmented, especially along the edges where blocks meet.
custom_77a73964.motivation: This is the backbone of Vermont's forest network that lets animals move across the state and into New Hampshire and Québec. It matters for daily movement, for young animals dispersing to find territory, for genetic exchange between populations, and for species shifting range as the climate warms. It covers about half of Thetford, so read it as the background the finer-scale layers sit inside rather than a designation on any one site; that is why it sits in the middle tier here despite the state calling it highest priority. The goal is to avoid permanently fragmenting these blocks (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).

custom_6c658a98.name: Top-Rated Soils, Open Land
custom_6c658a98.goal: Keep the town's best farmland that is already open available for farming.
custom_6c658a98.motivation: The soils the NRCS scores highest for crop production: agricultural value groups 1 and 2, with relative values of 100 and 97 on a 100-point scale (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils). These are already open land, so they can be farmed now without clearing. Open land is a field the town's inventory mapped from 2016 aerial imagery: hay, pasture, corn, other crops, and grassy openings of at least an acre, some of which may be large lawns (Thetford Natural Resource Inventory, 2021). These open fields also carry grassland birds that have declined regionally, including bobolink and eastern meadowlark, which nest successfully only where mowing waits until after August 1 (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).

custom_d324ef92.name: Second Tier Crossings
custom_d324ef92.goal: Keep these road crossings permeable where forest continues on both sides.
custom_d324ef92.motivation: Crossings with average connectivity on the study's regionally or locally important road sections, and the best-rated crossings on its potentially regionally important ones. Individually lower stakes than the top tier, but together they keep the town permeable, letting animals reach feeding, breeding and overwintering habitat within Thetford rather than only passing through it. From the 2025 Thetford wildlife road crossing study.
custom_d324ef92.how_built: Tiered by the study's road-section class and connectivity rating, as explained under Top Tier Crossings; the exact rule below lists which crossings fall in this tier.

custom_b38dc1ed.name: Productive Soils, Open Land
custom_b38dc1ed.goal: Keep good farmland that is already open available for farming.
custom_b38dc1ed.motivation: Important farmland soils with lower NRCS scores: agricultural value groups 3 to 7, with relative values from 84 down to 57 (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils). They include much of the town's prime soil, which the NRCS scores below its best soil of statewide importance. These are already open fields in the town's inventory, mapped from 2016 aerial imagery (Thetford Natural Resource Inventory, 2021), so they rank alongside top-rated soil that isn't open: one is the better soil, the other is ready to farm.

custom_65d165d2.name: Other Top-Rated Soils
custom_65d165d2.goal: Keep the town's best farmland soils available, including where the land isn't open today.
custom_65d165d2.motivation: Soils in the NRCS's two highest agricultural value groups, with relative values of 100 and 97, that the town's inventory did not map as an open field, such as forest. They rank below open top-rated soil because farming them would first mean clearing it, but the soil is no less capable: the NRCS groups soils by their characteristics, limitations and potential for crop production, assuming any corrective measures they need, such as drainage, can be applied (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils).

custom_84edb850.name: Other Productive Soils
custom_84edb850.goal: Keep good farmland soils available for the long term.
custom_84edb850.motivation: Soils in agricultural value groups 3 to 7 that the town's inventory did not map as an open field, such as forest. They rank lowest here on both counts — a lower crop-production score, and land that would need clearing to farm — but every one is rated prime or of statewide importance (NRCS, Farmland Classification Systems for Vermont Soils), and Vermont's Act 250 reviews soils of prime, statewide and local importance under Criterion 9(B), so they remain a conservation target. Thetford has no soils of local importance, so the four layers in this map cover every soil the NRCS rates as important farmland in town.

custom_bb4680ce.name: Important Wetlands
custom_bb4680ce.goal: Avoid any development, clearing, filling or drainage in the wetlands Vermont has mapped as state-significant.
custom_bb4680ce.motivation: Wetlands the town cannot replace: rare types such as the intermediate fen at Gillette Swamp, the wet clayplain forest at Connant Swamp and the sugar maple floodplain forest at Post Mills, plus the best examples of more common ones. Rare wetlands depend on particular soils, water chemistry and groundwater flow that can't be rebuilt once disturbed, so the aim is avoidance, not careful use.
custom_bb4680ce.how_built: The 13 wetland natural communities in Thetford mapped as state-significant by the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory (public version, data current to October 2026), buffered 50 ft as the Vermont Wetland Rules do for Class II wetlands. A community qualifies on rarity and quality: rare types (S1–S2) need a quality rank of A, B or C, uncommon and common types (S3–S4) an A or B, and the most common (S5) an A (Vermont Natural Heritage guidelines).

custom_0d7d7d49.name: Riparian Connectivity
custom_0d7d7d49.goal: Keep river and stream corridors forested, connected, and free to flood and meander.
custom_0d7d7d49.motivation: Riparian land does double duty: habitat for mink, otter, beaver and wood turtle, and the main connective tissue of an otherwise fragmented landscape. Forested banks stabilize soil, store floodwater, filter sediment and nutrients, and shade streams against warming. Vermont Conservation Design finds the corridor width needed for wildlife travel varies from about 100 ft on small streams to 600 ft or more on larger rivers, split either side of the water (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).
custom_0d7d7d49.how_built: Vermont Conservation Design's mapped riparian wildlife connectivity network in Thetford, as drawn by the state, with no buffer.

custom_0ce97644.name: Other Rare Species
custom_0ce97644.goal: Protect documented habitat for rare species that are not legally listed.
custom_0ce97644.motivation: Rare species are ones Vermont knows from only a handful of places, generally 20 or fewer (ranked S1 or S2); many are at the edge of their range or tied to scarce habitats. Unless listed as threatened or endangered they have no legal protection, which makes local attention matter more. Thetford has thirteen recorded occurrences: seven animals and six plants. The state withholds which species each one is.
custom_0ce97644.how_built: Occurrences in the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory (public version, data current to October 2026) of rare species not listed by Vermont or federally. Shapes are drawn exactly as the state publishes them, with no added buffer. About half are circles around a single observation, sized to how precisely it was located; the state notes a population may extend beyond what is mapped (Natural Heritage data guidelines).

custom_485e642b.name: Uncommon Species
custom_485e642b.goal: Keep the habitat of Thetford's uncommon species in mind when land changes.
custom_485e642b.motivation: Uncommon species (ranked S3, known from roughly 21 to 100 places in Vermont) are not rare, but are limited by scarce or shrinking habitat and could become rare. Thetford has fourteen recorded occurrences: eleven animals and three plants. The state withholds which species each one is.
custom_485e642b.how_built: Occurrences in the Vermont Natural Heritage Inventory's uncommon species layer (public version, data current to October 2026). Shapes are drawn exactly as the state publishes them, with no added buffer. About half are circles around a single observation, sized to how precisely it was located; the state notes a population may extend beyond what is mapped (Natural Heritage data guidelines).

custom_79610eba.name: Priority Connectivity Blocks
custom_79610eba.goal: Keep the rest of Thetford's forest network unfragmented.
custom_79610eba.motivation: The forest blocks the state rates Priority rather than Highest Priority are still part of the network that lets animals move across Vermont: they fill in between the larger blocks and keep the whole connected. Fragmenting them with roads or development narrows the routes wildlife have left (Vermont Conservation Design, Summary Report).

custom_d2593f87.name: Third Tier Crossings
custom_d2593f87.goal: Keep road crossings in mind where wildlife still crosses, even if less successfully.
custom_d2593f87.motivation: Crossings rated below average for connectivity on the study's regionally or locally important road sections, and average crossings on its potentially regionally important ones. Lower ratings reflect less roadside cover, harder terrain, more disturbance or less observed wildlife activity; these are places where improving conditions could matter. From the 2025 Thetford wildlife road crossing study.
custom_d2593f87.how_built: Tiered by the study's road-section class and connectivity rating, as explained under Top Tier Crossings; the exact rule below lists which crossings fall in this tier.

custom_49576c00.name: Deer Wintering Areas
custom_49576c00.goal: Keep the softwood cover that deer depend on in winter intact and connected.
custom_49576c00.motivation: Deer wintering areas are the patches of dense softwood (hemlock, balsam fir, red spruce or white pine) where white-tailed deer gather when snow is deep. Near the northern edge of the species' range, these yards decide whether deer get through hard winters, so Vermont treats them as important wildlife habitat under Act 250 and other regulations. Softwood cover takes decades to grow back, so losing the canopy or the travel lanes between yards can take an area out of use for a long time (VT Fish & Wildlife, Deer Wintering Areas).
custom_49576c00.how_built: Every deer wintering area the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources has mapped and approved in Thetford, as drawn by the state, with no buffer.
